articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications' (Digest No.64)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Describes work to develop methods for detecting and locating faults in analogue circuits which use minimal probing and only voltage measurements. The method developed uses only descriptions of the correct behaviour so that provided the description is appropriately constrained, any type of fault is detectable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fault diagnosis and on condition maintenance of a combined heat and power unit
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Describes an expert system involved in fault diagnosis for a combined heat and power unit. The traditional expert system approach need not be restricted to failure driven maintenance systems employing troubleshooting techniques. On the contrary predictive maintenance proves equally amenable to solution via an expert systems approach. Such systems by their very nature need to have the ability to employ deep reasoning when necessary. For this reason a causal or functional model of the engine is a prerequisite.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of knowledge based systems within the proposed telecommunications management network (TMN) environment to support fault diagnosis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Examines the use of a knowledge based system to model the diagnosis of faults in digital telecommunications transmission networks. The alarm surveillance network assumes the functionality and architecture of CCITT recommendations M.30 and G.771. A digital private circuit network is used as a vehicle to test the model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An expert system for production fault diagnosis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Explores the underlying basis of the fault finding process for electronic systems and maps the development of an expert system for inertial navigation systems production fault diagnosis. A computer based expert system has been implemented based on both surface level rules and on a knowledge of structure. General fault finding rules are defined and interviews with a test engineer conducted to provide unit specific fault finding rules. Prolog was chosen for system implementation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using qualitative reasoning for diagnostic applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Explores one way in which expert systems can be given domain knowledge to enable them to generate new diagnostic rules in the same way as human experts. This involves building a model of the domain and then comparing that model with the real world and accounting for the differences. Encouraging results have been documented for such diverse domains as electronic circuits, photocopiers and mechanical devices such as doorlocks. The last of these is used to illustrate the principles of the field. Qualitative modelling is a particular technique for building such models. The paper describes why it is both useful and limited, and explores principled ways of overcoming its limitations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diagnostic reasoning as an integration of experience-based and model-based reasoning
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Starts by considering several general issues involved in diagnostic reasoning. In particular, four main issues are addressed. These include the underlying assumptions of the system being diagnosed, the generation of fault hypotheses, the verification of fault hypotheses, and the management of the undecidability problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fault diagnosis prototype for Ethernet LANs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Describes a prototype of a fault diagnosis expert system for a chosen set of hardware and software faults on a LAN. The system uses a declarative model of the structure of the network to isolate the fault. This is not just a passive model: it provides the interface to the live network for gathering test data. The system's knowledge of tests is stored in the test objects, particularly in the select methods, which are able to choose appropriate parameters to each test and estimate its usefulness. One strategy for fault diagnosis is described and a number of extensions to the basic system, including the declarative representation of a selection of different diagnosis strategies, are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: FAUST: an expert system for diagnosing faults in an electricity supply system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: Gives a short account of a research project, funded by the IED, which is now in its fourth year. Its title is FAUST, and it is a real-time knowledge-based system whose task is to diagnose faults which occur in the electricity supply grid at area level (particularly, in its present form, at the 132 kV level). The paper concentrates on the developments which have been incorporated into the current version, known as FAUST 2.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The EXPOSER system and fault diagnosis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: A local firm manufactures a range of electronic banking equipment (terminals). For any particular piece of equipment a standard sequence of tests is carried out on the completed item before it is shipped to the customer. If any of these is failed then diagnostic action is taken, normally taking the form of 'module substitution', to determine the faulty module. In the case of a faulty item repair is carried out (usually module replacement) and it is resubmitted for testing. The company wanted assembly line workers rather than engineers to be able to carry out these test and diagnosis procedures. It was felt that a PC based system to guide such personnel through these procedures would be appropriate. EXPOSER (expert on the origin of system errors) was written in an attempt to fill this need. EXPOSER is written in PROLOG to run an IBM PC with a minimum of 640 K of RAM.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An expert system generating explanation for fault diagnosis in a water rig system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Expert Systems for Fault Diagnosis in Engineering Applications
abstract: A project is underway to construct an IKBS for fault diagnosis in a process control system able to cope with both single and multiple faults, and which generate explanation describing the reasoning underlying a particular diagnosis. The diagnosis system here uses qualitative modelling and deep knowledge techniques in which a behavioural and structural model based on the physics of a system, is formulated instead of using the classical shallow knowledge paradigm (using rules for example). So given knowledge of the input to a device and an understanding of how it is supposed to work, then expectation about its actual behaviour can be generated. Then a comparison between these two, specially the difference between them, provides the foundation of the trouble-shooter.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
